walkthroughs.body_html:
Rates of Reaction & Equilibrium — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Rates of Reaction & Equilibrium brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Rates of Reaction & Equilibrium.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which does NOT increase reaction rate?
options: Higher temperature
Smaller particles
Adding a catalyst
Lower concentration
raising the activation energy
lowering the activation energy
increasing reactant concentration
heating the system

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: The forward reaction stops once the reverse reaction begins.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.

mcqs.q: Does a catalyst affect the position of equilibrium?
options: A catalyst increases the yield by being consumed in the forward reaction only.
No — it speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but at the same position.
A catalyst shifts the equilibrium towards the products.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.

mcqs.q: At dynamic equilibrium, what is happening to the reactions?
options: Forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; concentrations remain constant.
A catalyst increases the yield by being consumed in the forward reaction only.
Both reactions stop because the system has reached balance.
The forward reaction stops once the reverse reaction begins.
